newsitem.title: USA: U.S. corp debt players retreat, quiet session seen.
newsitem.headline: U.S. corp debt players retreat, quiet session seen.

text.p: The corporate debt primary market was expected to see a quiet session on Friday as a weaker U.S. Treasury market triggered issuers to retreat, dealers said.
"I haven't heard a thing for today or next week," said one syndicate source. "The market is weaker ... most players took advantage of the improved tone yesterday to issue."
The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond was trading on Friday morning off 14/32 at 97-9/32 to yield 6.58 percent, the yield up slightly from 6.55 percent at Thursday's close.
On Thursday, the corporate market saw a slew of new issuance as rates improved and players rushed to square away business before the weekend, dealers said.
Wall Street firms sold about $2.5 billion in new corporate debt offerings on Thursday, dealers said, noting that the high-grade arena saw close to $1.0 billion in new supply.
Among the issues was Tandy Corp's $150 million 6.95 percent 10-year notes. The issue priced at a spread of 73 basis points and freed to trade at a 75 basis points bid, 72 offer, traders said.
Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc's $250 million 7.20 percent notes which priced at a spread of 94 basis points was seen trading at a 94 basis points bid, 93 offer, on the break, traders said.
Among other investment grade issuers, Liberty Property Trust sold $200 million in debt and ServiceMaster LP issued $300 million, players said.

In the junk arena, about $1.5 billion in new offerings came to market. Fox/Liberty Network priced the largest deal of the bunch, bringing $750 million in a two-part debt offering which was increased in size by $150 million to meet deamand.

Fox/Liberty's 10-year senior notes which priced at par to yield 8.875 percent, were seen trading Friday morning at 99-1/2 bid, 99-3/4 offer. The zero coupon tranche priced at 62.291 was seen trading at 61-3/4 bid, 62-1/2 offer, traders said.
Among other deals, Capstar Hotel's 12-year 8.75 percent notes were quoted at 100 bid, 100-1/4 offer, after pricing at 99.866 to yield 8.77 pecent, traders said.

Seperately, AMG Data Services reported that investors pulled money out of U.S. high-yield bond mutual funds in the latest week, causing cash flow figures to turn negative for the first time since May.

AMG reported net cash outflows of $25.2 million for the week ended August 13. The last time the weekly figure was negative was on 28, when the mutual fund tracking company reported net outflows of $31.6 million from U.S. junk funds.

Sam DeRosa-Farag, head of high-yield bond strategy at Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp, said the recent sell-off in the Treasury market was the most likely cause of the reversal in junk bond cash flows.
"What you see is a pattern in which the high-yield market is very sensitive to interest rates and the interest rate outlook," he said.

"As soon as you have serious Treasury volatility, you find that all other instruments such as high-yield bonds and equities will start to experience above-average volatility, with comparable uncertainty," he added.
On July 30, the yield on the benchmark 30-year bond was at 6.30 percent, its lowest level in over a year. Since then rates have backed up, making it more expensive for issuers to finance debt.
Meanwhile, the Dow rallied 29 percent from its 1997 closing low on April 11 at 6391.69 to its record closing high August 6 at 8259.31.
However, since August 11 the Dow has remained below the 8,000 area as fears of higher interest rates coupled with persistent declines in the bond marketa have pressured blue chips lower.
Early Friday afternoon, the Dow stood off 92 points from Thursday's close, at 7849.
(( -- Nancy Leinfuss, U.S. corporate bond unit,
